comments.author: @wpelfeta
comments.text:
The term "metagame" originated from Starcraft, where pros would use "metagame" tactics to gain an advantage. In those days "metagame" meant "beyond the game". Originally, it would be things like you know strategy A is popular currently, so you use strategy B to counter it before even seeing it in game. Thus, using your knowledge from "beyond the game" to influence your play within the game. However, this term became bastardized through frequent misuse and eventually came to mean almost the exact opposite of its origin. These days "meta" just means the commonly accepted rules of engagement (or as you put it, the "most effective tactics available"). But historically, metagaming would have meant knowing the commonly accepted rules of engagement, and, specifically, "metagaming" would have been the act of countering it or getting an advantage by knowing what everyone else is doing. So in your example, Tim Feriss was metagaming by doing the dehydration cut. But once it became popular, that strategy is no longer "metagaming" but rather just becomes part of the game.

All this to say... I'm just being pedantic. The definition of metagaming has changed, and these days the "meta" does refer the currently dominant strategy. Anyway, just wanted to explain where the term "meta" came from.

comments.author: @faithfocals
comments.text:
I'm a creator too, so I understand the urge to do what's necessary to game the algorithm. This comment isn't coming from a place of ire, it's just contributing to the conversation.

I think the reason clickbait gets backlash (as opposed to, say, posting videos, which is another really effective way to get seen on YouTube) is that clickbait really does depend on a little bit of deception in order to work. If people didn't click on "shocking" videos, clickbait wouldn't be a meta. By putting "Shocking" in every title regardless of the content, you're manipulating your viewership. When you post videos, to use my analogy, you give the viewer what they're looking for. But if you advertise something "Shocking" and it's you drawing a little bear for an hour, to use your analogy, you're not giving the viewer what they're looking for, and they feel manipulated.

If that's an acceptable risk for you, good game. Personally, it teaches me that you never have anything shocking or stunning to present, so I might click on fewer of your videos as I become more familiar with your content. (That said, you generally produce great content, so I doubt you'll lose me completely as long as I'm interested in AI.) As you pointed out, this meta will run out. When it does, you might be left with an audience that doesn't presume you care about their best interests.

Thanks for the video. Apologies Wes, But I have to disagree re: Sora. It is Not more accurately a physics simulator. It has almost no concept the underlying physics in its current state... because its training is simply not adequate for that level of abstraction where it can make inductive reasoning about the laws of physics based on the experience it has with its observations, but sure it could "gain" that ability over time with improvements. But as it stands calling it a world simulator / physics simulation tool is sort of like saying tetris is a gravity simulator. Sure, things fall in tetris, but that doesn't mean it understands gravity. Same thing with Sora. It is simply a simulation of the video training. The water might "look" like it is doing the right thing, but that is only at the most superficial level. 
   But, it would be "unfair" to simply leave my opinion without any sort of measuring test -- One set of basic criteria: Does it understand mass? Does it understand Inertia? Does it understand that objects collide? Does it understand any of the basics like "acceleration"? Friction?
   For collisions: When humans are walking in the videos, they frequently collide in the background and walk thru things. If it had a real world understanding of the physics it would know that this could not happen. You don't see it happen too much in the foreground, but in crowds you see weird things like that. In a way it is a lot like an "observer" -- it observes stuff and then replicates it. But, when asked to replicate something it hasn't seen, it will not understand it and likely will simply mess up the physics. 

   For Inertia, Collision, and Acceleration: The scene where construction workers are "working" with heavy machinery -- drop it down to very few frames per sec and at ~ 459 in the video shows a Forklift -- the wheels don't move right, there is no friction between the wheel and the ground, it nearly hits a guy but has zero inertia, it Melts and turns as it nearly collides... and goes from "forward" to "rightward" simultaneously melting in the direction it is traveling without actually changing the "forks" in the direction it is moving in. 

So no... it is nothing like a physics simulator... (perhaps in a few generations, tho).
   Regarding "it has to understand some stuff" -- yes, I do agree it understands "some stuff" (if you want to call it understanding). At the most basic level tho, that "understanding" is a "false" understanding -- because a video isn't a good representation of physical reality... ie, it almost ONLY ever shows surface topology. So, in its "current" iteration, it will fail horribly at physics. Can it progress to a better understanding... absolutely. But, in order for that to happen -- they will have to do much more extensive training. Just "replicating" a few things at the superficial level might suggest there is an emergent property at work, and there might be... but it doesn't mean it understands physics "now"...
   Regarding your request to Ignore your titles, if you liked the content... "sure, I can sort of ignore the hyperbole"... its just that I already enjoy your content, provided that the "thing" you claim in the title... is somewhere in that content. So, Arm your Sword of Shock and Shield of Awe... whatever... just please include what it was you shocked and awed about in the content somewhere.
